newsitem.title: ITALY: Body of executed American reaches Sicily.
newsitem.headline: Body of executed American reaches Sicily.

text.p: The body of Joseph O'Dell, a convicted murderer and rapist who was executed in the United States last week, arrived on Wednesday in Palermo, the city which took his appeals for mercy to its heart.

Although he had no Italian blood, O'Dell's case aroused overwhelming public sympathy in a nation which strongly opposes the death penalty. Italy's prime minister and president had joined the Pope in vain appeals for his life.

An airport official said the corpse would be taken directly to the Santa Maria di Gesu cemetery in Palermo, which made O'Dell an honorary citizen and where he was due to be buried following a religious ceremony on Thursday morning.

O'Dell's widow Lori Urs, a lifelong friend who married him hours before his execution in Virginia last Wednesday, was on the plane bringing the body, along with his spiritual advisor Sister Helen Prejean.

The two women were greeted by local government officials but declined to talk to reporters during the 45 minute Alitalia flight from Rome, saying they would hold a news conference after Thursday's burial.
Palermo, more than perhaps any other city, led the calls for clemency for O'Dell, who was executed by lethal injection for the 1985 rape and murder of Helen Schartner.
The city made him an honorary citizen and its mayor, Leoluca Orlando, flew to Virginia last Monday to ask State governor George Allen to reconsider O'Dell's fate.
O'Dell responded to Palermo's warmth by asking for his body to be buried there -- a request that was granted.
But not everybody in Italy was happy with the decision to honour a convicted rapist and murderer with a long criminal record and no known ties with Italy.
"It's a grotesque farce," senator Valentino Martelli of the rightist Alianza Nazionale told the national parliament in Rome on Wednesday.
"We're amazed that not a single member of the government has done anything to block this gross and disgusting spectacle which has seriously damaged the image of our country.
Prime Minister Romano Prodi, who along with Pope Jean Paul II appealed for O'Dell to be spared, has distanced himself from Thursday's ceremony in Palermo.
The Pope, who met Urs in Rome earlier on Wednesday, has said nothing in public about Palermo's decision to honour a man regarded by many in the United States as a heartless killer.
Urs also addressed a group of Italian deputies during her stopover in Rome.
"Joseph must continue to be a symbol of the injustice of capital punishment in the United States and in the rest of the world," she told them.
"When (the death penalty) is abolished we will know that Joseph did not die in vain."
